overview: I4202 is the FMS arrival event: build and verify the route, load procedures from the current database, manage discontinuities and crew edits, then fly the RNAV arrival or approach with chart discipline instead of blind magenta-line trust. The event standard is to make the FMS support the clearance while the chart, ATC clearance, and aircraft state remain the controlling references.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: An FMS flight plan is one active route containing an origin airport, destination airport, and at least one waypoint; two routes may be loaded, but only one can be active.

children.text: Create or recall the route on the ROUTE page, review and edit the waypoint sequence on the LEGS page, and add SID, STAR, and approach procedures from the DEP/ARR page.

Use the current navigation database for procedures. A SID, STAR, approach, or transition should be retrieved by procedure name and verified against the chart, not hand-built as a loose list of waypoints.
The flight number on MFD ROUTE page 1 is the Flight ID transmitted to ATC through Mode S.
Local habit may reserve RTE 1 for the primary route and RTE 2 for the filed alternate, but the aircraft truth is that only the active route drives navigation.
During edits, expect a flashing green EXEC cue on PFD/NAV and an inverse cyan MOD cue on the LEGS page.
Press EXEC on the UFCP to make the modification active, or ERASE before execution to discard the pending modification.
Only one cockpit can edit the flight plan at a time. If the other cockpit tries to edit before EXEC, the FMS can show ENTRY CONFLICT.
The active TO waypoint and active leg are highlighted magenta; inactive-route waypoint names are cyan. Use color as a cue, then verify the actual leg data.
Review the LEGS page before EXEC for waypoint order, course, distance, altitude/speed advisory data, and procedure leg type.
Route discontinuities are inserted when the FMS cannot build a continuous path, such as after some direct-to, procedure, or route insertions.
Close discontinuities only after verifying the chart and clearance support the connection. A clean magenta line is not proof that the route is legal.
Any waypoint may be made the current TO waypoint by moving it to the TO position, but doing so removes intervening waypoints and can bypass restrictions.
FMS turn anticipation can roll in or out up to about 4 degrees per second and up to 30 degrees AOB, but the pilot is still responsible for airspace, restrictions, and clearance compliance.
For SID selection, choose the runway, SID, and transition from DEP/ARR, then review the first legs and restrictions before EXEC.
For STAR selection, choose the destination arrival and transition, review all legs and restrictions, close only valid discontinuities, then execute.
For approach selection, choose the approach and transition from DEP/ARR, verify the initial, final, and missed-approach legs, then execute.
For holding, use the HOLD page or the /H scratchpad method on the desired fix, then verify direction, leg length or timing, and the clearance that authorizes the hold.

items.text: FMS arrivals use the FMS to transition from en route structure to a STAR, TAA, RNAV approach, or vector-to-final setup while the chart and clearance remain controlling.

children.text: A STAR clearance authorizes the published lateral route and any assigned restrictions, but published expect altitudes or speeds are planning information until ATC assigns or clears them.
A TAA transitions aircraft from RNAV en route structure into protected terminal airspace and provides at least 1000 feet of obstacle clearance within the depicted sector.
Being cleared direct to an IAF or IF/IAF without an approach clearance does not authorize descent to the lower TAA altitude.
Once cleared for the approach and inside the applicable TAA sector, descend no lower than the depicted minimum altitude for that sector unless ATC assigns something more restrictive.
The T-6B is certified to fly RNAV (GPS) approaches to LNAV MDA minimums only; do not use LNAV/VNAV, VNAV, or LPV minimums.
GPS stand-alone approaches require the procedure to be loaded from the current database; underlying ground-based NAVAIDs are not required, but may be monitored when available.
GPS overlay of non-precision procedures is limited to authorized overlays retrievable from the current database. Localizer, LDA, and SDF procedures are not authorized as GPS overlays.
For any RNAV DP, STAR, or approach, the loaded FMS procedure must match the charted procedure and clearance.
Use LDDHA: Load the GPS approach, Direct to the IAWP, Display source to FMS, Hold/HILO or missed approach set correctly, and Approach mode verified.
If radar-vectored to final, make the FAWP the active leg and extend the inbound final approach course as required, then comply with vectoring instructions until cleared for the approach.
Slow to 150 KIAS within 5 NM of the IAWP when flying the full published entry.
Transition to before-approach configuration within 5 NM of the FAWP.
Expect the HSI scale-change cue near 3 NM from the FAWP and verify APR annunciation near 2 NM from the FAWP.
At the FAWP, execute the 6 Ts as applicable, then descend using about 20% torque, 120 KIAS, and a stabilized rate not greater than 1000 FPM.
Level at MDA and fly to the MAWP; do not let the FMS lead you into an early descent below MDA.
If the runway environment is not in sight or landing is unsafe at the MAWP, execute the missed approach.
The FMS will not automatically sequence the missed approach at the MAWP; once stabilized in the climb and clean, select MISS APR and EXEC as required to sequence the published missed.
If GPS integrity is lost before the FAWP, transition to an authorized backup approach if available.
If no backup is available before the FAWP, continue on course to the FAWP, maintain the FAWP altitude to the MAWP, then execute the missed approach.

If GPS integrity is lost inside the FAWP, treat it as serious: transition to an authorized backup if available, climb to missed-approach altitude, continue tracking to the MAWP, and inform ATC as soon as practical.
Common errors are loading the wrong approach or transition, misusing TAA/feeder altitudes, late BAC, missing APR mode, and using the wrong minimums.

studyNotes.summary: Use the FMS deliberately: build and verify the route, execute only chart-supported changes, then fly FMS arrivals with TAA, APR-mode, GPS-integrity, and missed-approach sequencing discipline.

summary: FMS route/procedure management, RNAV arrival setup, GPS approach limits, and missed-approach sequencing.
